item.title: The coordinator pattern's quiet memory leak
item.description:
Here is the coordinator every UIKit app grows into. A parent holds its children in an array and starts a new one whenever it pushes a flow.

protocol Coordinator: AnyObject {
 var childCoordinators: [Coordinator] { get set }
 func start()
}

final class AppCoordinator: Coordinator {
 var childCoordinators: [Coordinator] = []
 let nav: UINavigationController

 init(nav: UINavigationController) { self.nav = nav }

 func showProfile() {
 let child = ProfileCoordinator(nav: nav)
 childCoordinators.append(child) // retained here
 child.start() // pushes ProfileViewController
 }
}

A user opens a profile, taps back, opens another, taps back, and does it ten more times. Question before you scroll: how many ProfileCoordinator instances are alive now?

item.title: Why your SwiftUI view model keeps resetting
item.description:
Here is a view model that fetches a list of jokes. It compiles, it passes review, and it ships in a lot of apps.

final class JokeViewModel: ObservableObject {
 @Published var jokes: [Joke] = []
 private var cancellables = Set<AnyCancellable>()

 func fetch() {
 JokeService.fetchJokes()
 .sink(receiveCompletion: { _ in }, receiveValue: { [weak self] in
 self?.jokes = $0
 })
 .store(in: &cancellables)
 }
}

struct JokeList: View {
 @ObservedObject var viewModel = JokeViewModel() // note this line

 var body: some View {
 List(viewModel.jokes) { Text($0.text) }
 .onAppear { viewModel.fetch() }
 }
}

Now put JokeList inside a parent that has a search field, and type one character.

item.title: How Swift and Objective-C see each other
item.description:
Your Swift class is public, the Objective-C file that needs it does #import "ShopKit-Swift.h", and the build fails: Cannot find interface declaration for 'OrderFormatter'. The class is right there in the same module, the header exists, and the compiler parsed it. So why is your class not in it?

Because the two languages do not read each other’s source. They meet through two generated artifacts pointing in opposite directions, and each one is gated by a build setting that has to be right. By the end you will know which artifact carries which direction, the setting that produces each, and why your @objc class can still go missing.

item.title: Why your xcconfig value gets ignored
item.description:
You move PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER into a shared .xcconfig so every target reads from one file. You build, and the bundle id is still the old value the .xcconfig was supposed to replace. The file is assigned to the right configuration. The syntax is correct. Xcode is reading it. And it loses anyway.

Why does a value you explicitly wrote in an .xcconfig get silently overridden by nothing you can see in the file?

item.title: Reading the build log for the slow line
item.description:
One-line change, incremental build, and one file sits at the compiler for forty seconds. The build log scrolls past a thousand lines and the only summary it gives you is CompileSwiftSources took a while. Which line? It will not say.

Somewhere in that file is an expression like this:

let label = "Order " + id + ": " + name + " x" + String(qty)
 + " = " + String(price * quantity) + " " + currencyCode

Reads fine. Compiles. And on its own it can cost the type-checker several seconds. The question is which expression, and the default log never points at it. By the end you will know the two flags that make the compiler name the slow line, and the one that names the slow phase.

item.title: Same arm64, two builds that will not mix
item.description:
A binary framework a vendor shipped links fine when you build for a device. Switch the destination to the simulator on your M-series Mac and the link dies:

Building for 'iOS-simulator', but linking in object file
(…/Analytics.framework/Analytics) built for 'iOS'

Both your Mac and the iPhone are arm64. lipo -info on that framework prints arm64. So why does the linker insist one arm64 object cannot go into the other arm64 build?

item.title: The build passed and the app still crashed on launch
item.description:
The build is green. Zero warnings. You launch on a device and it dies before the first frame:

dyld: Library not loaded: @rpath/PaymentsKit.framework/PaymentsKit
 Referenced from: /private/var/.../ShoppingApp.app/ShoppingApp
 Reason: image not found

The linker found PaymentsKit. The compiler was happy. So why can the app not find it two seconds later at launch?

Because a green build proves the linker resolved your symbols, not that the app can load at runtime. Those are two different jobs, run at two different times, and the gap between them is exactly where static-versus-dynamic, Embed & Sign, and @rpath live. By the end you will read that crash and know which checkbox is wrong.

item.title: Debug and Release run different code
item.description:
A crash report comes in from TestFlight. The stack points at a function that is green on every simulator run and every device debug session you can throw at it. You cannot reproduce it. The code looks correct.

func averageLatency(_ samples: [Int]) -> Int {
 assert(!samples.isEmpty, "never call this with no samples")
 return samples.reduce(0, +) / samples.count // crashes in Release, not Debug
}

Read it and answer: why does this survive every debug run and divide by zero in production?

item.title: When your incremental build lies
item.description:
Here is a Run Script phase that regenerates an API client from a spec file. It works. But every clean-looking incremental build takes four extra seconds, and once a week someone gets a stale client and loses an hour.

# Run Script phase: "Generate API client"
swift run codegen --input api-spec.yaml --output Generated/APIClient.swift

Two questions before we go on. Why does this script run on every build, even when nothing changed? And why, when the spec does change, does the app sometimes compile against the old generated file anyway?

item.title: Chat Uploads That Outlive the App
item.description:
The interview prompt: “Design media upload for a WhatsApp-style chat.” A user picks a 40MB video, sees a thumbnail with a progress ring, then switches to another app to take a call. iOS suspends your app, and may terminate it under memory pressure. When they come back, the video is sent. Nothing in that sentence is hard until the app leaves the foreground.

item.title: The Chat Outbox for Offline Sync
item.description:
The interview prompt is one line: “Design WhatsApp-style offline messaging for iOS.” You tap send on the subway, the message shows a clock, and three stops later it turns into a double tick. Simple to describe. The whole problem lives in what has to be true for that tick to be honest.

Here is the version most candidates draw first:

final class MessageQueue {
 private var messages: [Message] = []
 func enqueue(_ m: Message) { messages.append(m) }
 func dequeue() -> Message? { messages.isEmpty ? nil : messages.removeFirst() }
}

Spot the two bugs before reading on. One loses messages. The other duplicates them. By the end you will have the outbox and the client-side dedup key that kill both, and a status machine that can only move forward.

item.title: The reduce That's Secretly O(n²)
item.description:
map, filter, and reduce get recommended as the faster choice over a for loop. They do read better. Faster is the part that does not hold up, and one of them has a default that turns a one-line accumulation into O(n²) while sailing through review. By the end you will know which one, why, and the one-word change that fixes it.

“Functional is faster” is backwards

A for loop over an array is about as cheap as computing gets: one pass, one array, no intermediates. A chain of higher-order functions does the same logical work and allocates along the way.

item.title: How Closures Capture, and Why Your Screen Leaks
item.description: Push a screen, pop it, push it again, and watch deinit never fire while memory climbs. That is the most common memory bug in iOS, and it almost always comes down to one thing a closure does quietly: capture. A closure grabs the things it references and keeps them alive. Get that wrong with a closure that outlives the call, and you have a view controller that can never deallocate.

item.title: Copy-on-Write, and When Structs Bite
item.description:
“Use structs by default” is advice so repeated that nobody asks the obvious follow-up: what does the copy actually cost? Everyone can recite that structs copy and classes share. The part worth your attention is what “copy” means at runtime, when it is free, when it quietly is not, and the class of bug that shows up when you have lost track of which one you are holding.

We will assume you know the textbook difference. Assign a struct, you get an independent copy. Assign a class, both names point at the same instance. Here is everything past that.

item.title: What Swift's Optional Really Is
item.description:
How many states can a screen actually be in, and does its type let it represent states that mean nothing? That question is where optionals stop being about syntax.

Everyone meets Optional once, as “the box that might be empty,” then moves on to unwrapping. The parts that still bite years in are elsewhere: what Optional actually is, the two or three places it behaves in ways that surprise people, and the design call nobody frames at the syntax stage. When is an optional the right tool, and when is it a sign the problem has not been modeled yet?

item.title: Modeling the Current User Without a Global Singleton
item.description:
Almost every app has the line. User.current, or Session.shared, or AppState.user. A global you can reach from anywhere that holds the logged-in user. It is the most convenient object in the codebase on day one and, a year later, the most coupled. The profile module is usually where the rot shows up first, because profile screens read and write the current user more than anywhere else.

The real question is not what goes in the UserProfile module. It is how the current user gets modeled and reached, because that one decision is what keeps the app testable or slowly strangles it.

item.title: any vs some: what a protocol type costs
item.description:
Two functions do the same job over a list of activities. One takes [any LoggableActivity], the other is generic over [T]. They compile to very different machine code. Which one allocates a box per element, and which one gets the calorie math inlined?

protocol LoggableActivity {
 var caloriesBurned: Double { get }
}

func total(_ items: [any LoggableActivity]) -> Double { // A
 items.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.caloriesBurned }
}

func total<T: LoggableActivity>(_ items: [T]) -> Double { // B
 items.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.caloriesBurned }
}

Version A pays for a heap box and a dynamic call on every element. Version B specializes to the concrete type and often inlines the whole loop. By the end you will know what any actually stores, why some and generics are cheaper, and when the box is the right call anyway.

item.title: Where API-to-UI Data Flow Breaks
item.description:
Ask anyone to draw API-to-UI data flow and you get the same picture: networking fetches, a view model holds state, the view renders. Boxes and arrows, two minutes on a whiteboard. The diagram is never where data flow breaks. What breaks is everything the diagram hides.

item.title: Architecture for a Team Scaling 5 to 20
item.description: When a team is five people, architecture is a technical question. When it is twenty, it is mostly an organizational one, and the codebase will end up shaped like the org chart whether you plan for it or not. That last part is Conway’s law, and on a growing iOS team it stops being a fun aphorism and starts being the thing that decides whether your release train runs on time.

item.title: Using Cursor in a Flutter Workathon
item.description:
Forty-eight hours to rebuild a real production screen in Flutter, test it, and ship it for a panel review. Nine teams. We wrote about 10,000 lines in two days, let Cursor generate roughly 80% of it, and placed 2nd.

The score is not the interesting part. What breaks when you lean on an AI agent under real time pressure, on code with deeply nested logic, while making decisions fast, is. Every item below cost us time before it saved us any. What follows is the workflow we ended up with, and why each piece earned its place.

item.title: The Shared Module Trap in iOS Apps
item.description:
You change one line in Core and the whole app recompiles. Again. The feature modules were the easy half of modularization and they came out fine. The half quietly eating the payoff is the shared module: the Core, Common, or Shared target everything depends on.

It starts as obvious good sense (“don’t duplicate networking”) and ends as a second monolith wearing a module’s clothes. It fails in a few specific, predictable ways. Name them and the fix is a small set of structural rules, with a concrete payoff: that one-line change stops rebuilding the whole app.

item.title: How big is an enum with associated values?
item.description:
Here is a four-case enum for an image cell, the kind that ships in every feed. Right now the value is in the .idle case, holding nothing at all. How many bytes does that empty value occupy?

struct Bitmap { // 64 bytes, stored inline
 var pixels: (UInt64, UInt64, UInt64, UInt64,
 UInt64, UInt64, UInt64, UInt64)
}

enum ImageState {
 case idle
 case loading(progress: Double) // 8 bytes
 case ready(Bitmap) // 64 bytes
 case failed(code: Int) // 8 bytes
}

Most people answer “a few bytes, it’s empty.” The real answer is 72. By the end you will know why an idle enum carries the weight of its heaviest sibling, and the one keyword that cuts it back down.

item.title: What Modular iOS Actually Costs
item.description:
“Should we modularize the app?” gets argued like a values question, monolith for the scrappy, modules for the grown-ups. It is not a values question. Modularization buys specific things and costs specific things, both measurable, and the teams that get burned are the ones that paid the cost without checking whether they needed what it bought.

The usual pros-and-cons list (“easier to scale”, “more complex setup”) is too vague to decide with. Price it out instead.

item.title: Why UIKit Breeds Massive View Controllers
item.description:
Every iOS team eventually fights the same file. A view controller that started small and is now four figures of line count, the one nobody volunteers to touch. The usual explanation is discipline: someone got lazy, nobody refactored. That explanation is comfortable and mostly wrong.

Massive View Controller is not a discipline failure. It is what UIKit’s design pushes you toward by default. Understand the mechanism and you stop fighting symptoms. First, why the controller becomes a magnet. Then what each escape hatch actually costs, because none of them are free.

item.description:
Everything about Error Handling in Combine

In the previous article, while discussing the 5 essential caveats to remember to master Combine, we touched upon error handling briefly. In this article, we will dive deep into error handling in Combine, covering everything there is about built in error handling in Combine.

This article is part of a series where I dive deep into iOS concepts, exploring the smallest details often overlooked by typical articles. I aim to blend definitions with practical insights for a clear and actionable understanding. Whether you’re a seasoned developer or eager to learn, this series will provide the insights and skills needed to master these powerful frameworks. Let’s get started.

item.title: Mastering Swift Combine: 5 Essential Caveats to Remember
item.description:
Mastering Swift Combine: 5 Essential Caveats to Remember

Combine framework’s caveats: Learn key pitfalls and actionable insights for effective integration into your code.

Combine, Apple’s own reactive programming framework, holds immense potential. However, effectively using its capabilities demands one to be aware of specific caveats and pitfalls.

This article explores these caveats and provides actionable insights for integrating Combine effectively into your code. While some considerations here may seem intuitive, they are often overlooked until you grasp Combine thoroughly.
